# Topology, Statistical Parameter Mapping, and Surface Visualization

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This chapter is about how the shape of the brain — its folded, topologically
complex surface — shapes the choices we make when we smooth, average, and
visualize MRI data. The theme running through the chapter is that summary
statistics and generic image-processing operations (smoothing, volume
averaging, statistical parameter maps) can silently mix together signals from
neighboring but functionally unrelated tissue unless the underlying geometry
of cortex is respected.

## Why visualization matters

Anscombe's quartet is a classic illustration of a general danger: four data
sets with identical summary statistics (mean, variance, correlation) can look
completely different once plotted (@fig-ch67-anscombes-quartet). The same
danger applies to brain data — two very different patterns of activity or
tissue structure can share the same summary numbers, so visualizing the data
directly, not just its statistics, is an essential check.

![Anscombe's quartet: four data sets with the same summary statistics but
very different shapes when
plotted.](images/ch67/anscombes-quartet.png){#fig-ch67-anscombes-quartet}

Spatial resolution compounds this problem in the brain because of cortical
folding. Two points that are close together in physical (Euclidean) space can
be far apart along the folded cortical sheet, on opposite banks of a sulcus
(@fig-ch67-spatial-proximity-brain-folds). Any analysis that treats nearby
voxels as necessarily related is implicitly assuming a spatial smoothness that
the folded anatomy does not actually have.

![Spatial proximity in a volume does not imply proximity along the cortical
surface — brain folding brings distant regions of cortex physically close
together.](images/ch67/spatial-proximity-brain-folds.png){#fig-ch67-spatial-proximity-brain-folds}

## Topology and visualization

A single MR slice can cut across a sulcus twice, sampling both banks in the
same plane even though they are far apart along the cortical sheet — for
example, a coronal slice through the calcarine sulcus includes tissue from
both banks of the fold (@fig-ch67-calcarine-sulcus-mr-slice). This is the
concrete anatomical reason topology matters: the natural neighborhood
structure of the data is defined by the cortical surface, not by the
Euclidean geometry of the acquired volume.

![A coronal MR slice through the calcarine sulcus. The dotted line marks the
slice plane; an MR slice through the blue line would include parts of
opposite banks of the
sulcus.](images/ch67/calcarine-sulcus-mr-slice.png){#fig-ch67-calcarine-sulcus-mr-slice}

## Matching data methods to what you are studying

Thinking about the natural shape and organization of the problem you are
studying is important. Mathematical theorems about smoothing and averaging
are very useful, but every problem has its own special features, and being
sensitive to them is essential — spatial averaging in the brain is a good
example. A smoothing kernel applied in volume space averages together
whatever voxels fall within its radius, regardless of whether those voxels
belong to the same fold of cortex.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Grid of samples

![A regular grid of sample locations overlaid on an axial
slice.](images/ch67/smoothing-kernel-grid.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-kernel-grid-1}

## Selecting a pair of nodes

![Two neighboring grid nodes are
selected.](images/ch67/smoothing-kernel-node-pair.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-kernel-grid-2}

## The averaging kernel

![A circular averaging kernel is centered on the selected
nodes.](images/ch67/smoothing-kernel-averaging-circle.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-kernel-grid-3}
:::

The trouble is visible as soon as the kernel straddles a sulcus. Opposite
banks of a sulcus can be very close together in volume space yet functionally
distinct — one bank gray matter, the other white matter, or two banks
belonging to different functional maps — so opposite sides of sulci can't be
distinguished by a purely volumetric criterion
(@fig-ch67-opposite-sulci-sides-indistinguishable). The figure shown in-plane
is only a 2D cross-section; the averaging itself happens in the full 3D
volume, which makes the problem worse, not better.

![Opposite banks of a sulcus can be indistinguishable in volume space: white
matter and gray matter from both banks can fall within the same local
neighborhood. The averaging kernel operates in the volume even though only an
in-plane slice is
shown.](images/ch67/opposite-sulci-sides-indistinguishable.png){#fig-ch67-opposite-sulci-sides-indistinguishable}

Smoothing therefore averages together signal from tissue that may not belong
together at all (@fig-ch67-what-is-averaged-by-smoothing) — the same
sulcus-crossing problem, now shown as it would appear after a smoothing
kernel has been applied at several locations along a fold.

![What is actually averaged by smoothing: circles mark local regions where
the kernel mixes signal across opposite banks of a
sulcus.](images/ch67/what-is-averaged-by-smoothing.png){#fig-ch67-what-is-averaged-by-smoothing}

## Statistical parameter mapping

Statistical parameter maps (SPMs) render a statistical test (for example, a
t- or F-statistic computed at every voxel) as a color overlay on an anatomical
image. An older convention in the literature — one that can still be found in
some papers — displayed these overlays on a small number of 2D slices, which
is a visualization choice worth being alert to when reading older figures, since
it can make results look more (or less) spatially extensive than they are.

Spatial smoothing is applied before statistical testing for several distinct
reasons, and it is worth separating them out:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## (i) Matched filter theorem

By the matched filter theorem, the optimal smoothing kernel size matches the
expected spatial size of the effect being tested — smoothing at the wrong
scale reduces sensitivity.

![Motivation (i): the matched filter theorem sets the optimal smoothing
kernel size.](images/ch67/smoothing-matched-filter.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-rationale-1}

## (ii) Central limit theorem

By the central limit theorem, smoothing renders the noise distribution more
Gaussian, which helps satisfy the assumptions behind parametric statistical
tests.

![Motivation (ii): smoothing makes the error distribution more
normal.](images/ch67/smoothing-central-limit.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-rationale-2}

## (iii) Gaussian random field theory

Inferences about regional effects that rely on Gaussian random field theory
assume the underlying statistical field is smooth; explicit smoothing helps
satisfy that assumption.

![Motivation (iii): Gaussian random field theory assumes a smooth statistical
field.](images/ch67/smoothing-gaussian-random-field.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-rationale-3}

## (iv) Inter-subject averaging

When averaging across subjects — whose anatomy never aligns perfectly — more
aggressive smoothing (e.g., 8 mm in fMRI, 16 mm in PET) is often needed to
project individual results onto a common space.

![Motivation (iv): heavier smoothing compensates for imperfect inter-subject
alignment.](images/ch67/smoothing-intersubject-averaging.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-rationale-4}
:::

Each of these is a legitimate reason to smooth, but each also trades away
some spatial specificity — precisely the specificity that the sulcus-crossing
problem above shows can matter a great deal in folded cortex.

## Surface-based visualization

Visualization exists to communicate results clearly, and the choice of
surface matters as much as the statistics. The same activation can look very
different rendered on a small number of thick axial slices versus rendered on
a 3D cortical surface reconstruction (@fig-ch67-spm-quality-communication).

![The same statistical result shown (a) on thick axial slices and (b)
rendered on a 3D cortical surface — the surface rendering communicates the
spatial extent of the activation far more
clearly.](images/ch67/spm-quality-communication.png){#fig-ch67-spm-quality-communication}

Cortical surface projections are commonly shown from standard viewpoints,
such as the lateral surface and the ventral occipital surface, so that
results from different studies and subjects can be compared directly
(@fig-ch67-lateral-surface-projection, @fig-ch67-ventral-lateral-projection).

![A lateral surface projection of the cortex (data from Brunswick and
Paulesu).](images/ch67/lateral-surface-projection.png){#fig-ch67-lateral-surface-projection}

![A ventral occipital view of the cortical
surface.](images/ch67/ventral-lateral-projection.png){#fig-ch67-ventral-lateral-projection}

A concrete example of why this matters: interpreting results shown in a
conventional multi-slice format is hard, even for an experienced reader
(@fig-ch67-multislice-format-challenge). The same visual word form area data,
replotted on a 3D cortical surface reconstruction, is much easier to
interpret — the contrast showing an increasing response as a word form
becomes more visible is immediately legible as a single, spatially coherent
region rather than scattered patches across several slices
(@fig-ch67-word-form-area-3d-surface).

![Multi-slice format visualization is a challenge to understand: color
indicates stimulus eccentricity, but the spatial pattern is hard to read
across
slices.](images/ch67/multislice-format-challenge.png){#fig-ch67-multislice-format-challenge}

![The same data shown on a 3D surface reconstruction: the visual word form
area is much easier to see than in the multi-slice
view.](images/ch67/word-form-area-3d-surface.png){#fig-ch67-word-form-area-3d-surface}

## Building the cortical surface

To build a representation of the cortical surface, the anatomical MRI volume
is segmented into gray and white matter, and the boundary between them is
identified. A variety of software tools do this segmentation; here the
boundary is shown as identified by itkGray, one of several available
pipelines (others include FreeSurfer)
(@fig-ch67-itkgray-graywhite-boundary; @carman1995-corticalsurface;
@dale1999-corticalsurfacereconstruction; @fischl1999-corticalsurfacebased;
@wandell2000-visualization).

![Identifying the gray-white boundary in cortex using
itkGray.](images/ch67/itkgray-graywhite-boundary.png){#fig-ch67-itkgray-graywhite-boundary}

Automatic segmentation is an excellent first approximation and very useful in
practice (@fig-ch67-segmentation-first-approximation), but there are always
imperfections that need to be checked and, often, hand-corrected
(@fig-ch67-segmentation-imperfections).

![Automatic gray/white segmentation: an excellent first approximation and
very useful on its
own.](images/ch67/segmentation-first-approximation.png){#fig-ch67-segmentation-first-approximation}

![But there are always imperfections that need
checking.](images/ch67/segmentation-imperfections.png){#fig-ch67-segmentation-imperfections}

Once the voxels are classified as gray or white matter, they must be
connected into a well-formed graph before a surface mesh can be built. Gray
matter nodes are considered connected if they share a common parent voxel or
if their parents are connected, and the classification, connectivity, and
resulting cortical graph are all closely linked
(@fig-ch67-classification-connectivity).

![Classification, connectivity, and the resulting graph of gray-matter
nodes.](images/ch67/classification-connectivity.png){#fig-ch67-classification-connectivity}

A well-formed white-matter classification must also avoid topological defects
— cavities (holes enclosed by white matter) and handles (spurious
connections that create a loop where none should exist). The Euler number is
a standard way of detecting the presence of such defects
(@fig-ch67-euler-number-cavities-handles; @toriwaki-eulernumber).

![White matter topology: avoiding cavities and handles. The Euler number
detects topological defects in the classified
volume.](images/ch67/euler-number-cavities-handles.png){#fig-ch67-euler-number-cavities-handles}

## From classified voxels to a mesh

Graphics programs represent surfaces as meshes: a set of vertices (points)
and edges (connections between them). A mesh can be built directly from the
boundary of the classified white-matter voxels
(@fig-ch67-mesh-from-classified-voxels).

![Creating the surface mesh from classified
voxels.](images/ch67/mesh-from-classified-voxels.png){#fig-ch67-mesh-from-classified-voxels}

Representing the cortex as a mesh matters for more than visualization: the
same mesh that renders the surface for viewing (in tools such as MeshLab)
also encodes the gray-matter connectivity graph used for measurement, so a
properly connected mesh is required both for pictures that look right and for
distances and areas that are computed correctly
(@fig-ch67-importance-of-being-a-mesh).

![The importance of being a mesh: a single mesh structure supports both
visualization and correct gray-node
connectivity.](images/ch67/importance-of-being-a-mesh.png){#fig-ch67-importance-of-being-a-mesh}

A raw mesh built directly from voxel boundaries is jagged; 3D graphical tools
(such as VTK, the Visualization Toolkit) can smooth the mesh without
destroying the topological neighborhood relations of the surface
(@fig-ch67-smoothing-the-3d-mesh). Modern segmentation and meshing tools such
as itkGray increasingly build in this kind of anatomical and topological
knowledge automatically, though getting good results still requires practice
(@fig-ch67-itkgray-tissue-classification).

![Smoothing the 3D mesh with tools such as VTK, preserving the surface's
topological
properties.](images/ch67/smoothing-the-3d-mesh.png){#fig-ch67-smoothing-the-3d-mesh}

![Tissue classification tools such as itkGray incorporate increasingly
sophisticated anatomical
knowledge.](images/ch67/itkgray-tissue-classification.png){#fig-ch67-itkgray-tissue-classification}

## Curvature and extreme smoothing

Shading a rendered surface by local curvature makes the gyri and sulci easy
to read at a glance: curvature is inversely related to the radius of the
circle that best fits the local surface
(@fig-ch67-shading-surface-curvature). Even after very heavy smoothing, the
mesh's topology — its neighborhood connectivity — remains unchanged; only the
geometry (the shape) is altered, not the underlying graph structure
(@fig-ch67-extreme-smoothing-topology-unchanged).

![Shading the surface by curvature: high curvature marks tightly folded gyri
and sulci, low curvature marks flatter
regions.](images/ch67/shading-surface-curvature.png){#fig-ch67-shading-surface-curvature}

![Extreme smoothing changes the surface's shape but leaves its topology
unchanged.](images/ch67/extreme-smoothing-topology-unchanged.png){#fig-ch67-extreme-smoothing-topology-unchanged}

## Flat maps

Because the cortical sheet is topologically close to a 2D surface, it can be
cut and unfolded into a flat map — a representation that preserves
neighborhood relations along the cortical surface far better than any single
volumetric slice can. Flattened representations are especially useful for
displaying data that vary smoothly across the surface, such as eccentricity
maps from retinotopic mapping experiments
(@fig-ch67-eccentricity-maps, @fig-ch67-flat-map-views,
@fig-ch67-eccentricity-map-flattened).

![An eccentricity map shown on the folded cortical
surface.](images/ch67/eccentricity-maps.png){#fig-ch67-eccentricity-maps}

![A flat-map view of the brain
surface.](images/ch67/flat-map-views.png){#fig-ch67-flat-map-views}

![The same eccentricity map shown on the flattened
representation.](images/ch67/eccentricity-map-flattened.png){#fig-ch67-eccentricity-map-flattened}

No flattening is perfect, however. The cortical surface has intrinsic
curvature, which limits how well distances measured on the flattened image
can match true distances on the folded surface — even a surface that is
basically flat, and not strongly curved like a sphere, will not be perfectly
representable on a plane without some distortion
(@fig-ch67-intrinsic-curvature-limits). The next chapter takes up the
flattening procedure itself in detail.

![Intrinsic curvature limits how well distances on a flattened image can
match true distances on the cortical
surface.](images/ch67/intrinsic-curvature-limits.png){#fig-ch67-intrinsic-curvature-limits}
